forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Horsham's auditor expects a qualified opinion on 2025/26 accounts, after two disclaimed years
news_drafts.lead:
Horsham District Council's external auditor has told the Audit Committee it expects to give a qualified opinion on the council's 2025/26 accounts, meaning it could not fully sign them off. The auditor's report says it has substantially completed the audit, and "we expect to issue a qualified opinion", subject to outstanding procedures.

The accounts for the two previous years received no opinion at all. The auditor's table records both 2023/24 and 2024/25 as disclaimed, which means it did not give an opinion. It shows 2025/26 as the first year in which it anticipates a qualified opinion.

The same table sets out the auditor's expectation for later years. It shows an unqualified opinion, a full sign-off of the accounts, as possible by 2028/29. The papers do not say what is outstanding for 2025/26. The committee meets on 25 November.

news_drafts.headline: Horsham forecasts a £0.66m operational surplus for 2026/27, after £1.9m surplus in 2025/26
news_drafts.lead:
Horsham District Council is forecasting an operational surplus of £0.66m for the 2026/27 financial year. The figure is in its finance and performance report for the second quarter, prepared for the Finance and Performance Policy and Scrutiny Committee meeting on 2 November. The forecast was made at Month 6 of the year.

The report sets the figure beside last year's. The council's outturn (the actual figures once a year has ended) for 2025/26 was an operational surplus of £1.9m, and the paper says that surplus "was delivered". At Month 4 of 2025/26, the council had forecast a surplus of £0.53m.

The report also gives the council's overall funding position for 2026/27, which is forecast at a £0.34m surplus. That figure is after budgets of £0.39m carried over from 2025/26.

news_drafts.headline: Reorganized parishes budget £202,000 for neighbourhood wardens and triple youth work spending
news_drafts.lead:
The reorganized parish council formed from three separate authorities is planning significant service expansions as it sets its budget for 2027/28. Neighbourhood warden costs more than double to £202,498, including provision for two additional staff members. Youth work spending increases tenfold to £60,000 from £6,000. The new unified authority, which will employ 11 staff including clerks and administrators at a cost of £559,000, is anticipated to hold £210,000 in reserves sourced from North Horsham Parish Council. However, residents face sharply divergent impacts on their precepts: Roffey Parish residents face a 36 per cent reduction of £26.89 on a Band D property, while Horsham Town Council residents see a 15 per cent decrease and North Horsham residents a 3 per cent rise. The budget provisions £10,000 for system harmonization between the previously separate parishes.

findings.paper_title: Statements updated for 2025-26 with audit adjustments draft v2
findings.headline: The Government's fair funding review 2.0 and the reset of the business rates retention system gave the Council some certainty for the medium term.
findings.detail: The going concern note says these changes provide some certainty for the medium term. It says the council still estimates budget gaps of £1m in 2028/29 and £5m by 2029/30.
findings.matters: A council's view of medium-term funding certainty after the funding reforms is the point other councils will compare when they assess their own position.
findings.quote: The impact of the Government fair funding review 2.0 and the reset of the business rates retention system provided the Council with some certainty for the medium term

findings.paper_title: Statements updated for 2025-26 with audit adjustments draft v2
findings.headline: The Council held a cash balance of £20.7m at the end of May 2026, plus £20.5m in liquid pooled funds investments.
findings.detail: The going concern note says the cash flow forecast covers twelve months beyond signing of the accounts, to 31 December 2027. It says the council would not run out of cash in a stressed case where income is constrained and costs are unplanned.
findings.matters: The stated cash and liquid pooled fund balances, and the stress test to December 2027, are the figures a lender or finance director would use to judge short-term liquidity.
findings.figures: £20.7m cash balance at end of May 2026; £20.5m liquid pooled funds investments
findings.quote: The Council had a cash balance of £20.7m at the end of May 2026

findings.paper_title: Statements updated for 2025-26 with audit adjustments draft v2
findings.headline: The number of permanent employees rose to 440.8 FTE at 31 March 2026, from 404.6 FTE a year earlier, to recruit for the domestic food waste service.
findings.detail: The narrative attributes the increase to recruitment for the domestic food waste service, which began in March 2026. Sickness absence fell to 4.84 days per FTE from 5.67 days, and remains below the 7-day target.
findings.matters: A 36.2 FTE rise linked to a single new statutory service shows the workforce cost of that service, which other councils will face when they introduce it.
findings.figures: 440.8 FTE at 31 March 2026; 404.6 FTE at 31 March 2025; 4.84 sickness days per FTE (5.67 in 2024/25); 7-day target
findings.quote: The number of permanent employees was 440.8 FTE at 31 March 2026 (404.6 at 31 March 2025)

findings.paper_title: Statements updated for 2025-26 with audit adjustments draft v2
findings.headline: An average of 41 households were placed in bed and breakfast accommodation during 2025/26, against a target of 30.
findings.detail: The narrative says demand has increased, with more individuals presenting as homeless. It also says delays by registered providers in completing void maintenance have slowed the flow of households out of temporary accommodation.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs are a growing budget pressure for councils, and the 41 households against a target of 30 is the council's own measure of that pressure.
findings.figures: 41 households on average in B&B (41.25 in table); 31.25 in 2024/25; 38 in 2023/24; target 30
findings.quote: Throughout the year an average of 41 households have been placed in B&B accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Statements updated for 2025-26 with audit adjustments draft v2
findings.headline: The pre-audit local authority error rate was 0.23%, against a 0.40% target, and the indicator is set at red.
findings.detail: The narrative says extrapolated errors found during the audit are more likely than not to push the rate over the lower threshold. That has happened in two of the last three years, although there was no subsidy loss in 2024/25.
findings.matters: The error rate drives housing benefit subsidy loss, and a finance director at another council would check whether their pre-audit rate is similarly close to the threshold.
findings.quote: the likelihood of extrapolated errors identified during the audit are more likely than not to push the error rate over the lower threshold
